faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions for Travelers in Morocco
faq.q1: Do I need an international driver's license to rent a car in Morocco?
faq.a1: Most rental agencies and checkpoints accept national driver's licenses written in Latin script (EU, UK, US, Canada). An International Driving Permit is recommended if your license uses a non-Latin script.
faq.q2: What are the dress codes when visiting medinas and rural villages?
faq.a2: In urban tourist hubs like Marrakech or Agadir beach resorts, casual summer wear is fine. However, in traditional medinas, religious sites, and Atlas villages, modest clothing covering shoulders and knees is appreciated.
faq.q3: Are credit cards widely accepted, or should I carry cash?
faq.a3: Major hotels, modern restaurants, and official shops accept credit cards. Cash in Moroccan Dirham (MAD) is essential for souks, taxis, tips, small shops, and desert or mountain oases.
faq.q4: Is Morocco safe for tourists and solo travelers?
faq.a4: Yes, Morocco is generally considered safe for tourists. Watch out for unofficial guides and persistent vendors in medinas, and use official taxis or ride-hailing apps. Avoid walking alone in poorly lit alleyways at night.
faq.q5: How can I get a SIM card and internet access in Morocco?
faq.a5: You can buy a SIM card upon arrival at the airport (Orange, Maroc Telecom, or Inwi). Tourist packages are inexpensive and include plenty of data. You can also activate roaming or use an eSIM if supported.
faq.q6: Do I need a visa to enter Morocco?
faq.a6: Citizens from the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, and many other countries do not need a visa for stays up to 90 days. Always double-check current requirements based on your nationality.
faq.q7: What is the best time of year to visit Morocco?
faq.a7: Spring (March–May) and Autumn (September–November) offer the best temperatures. Summer is hot inland but ideal along the Atlantic coast. Winter is mild in cities but cold in the Atlas, where snow may fall.
faq.q8: Can you drink tap water in Morocco?
faq.a8: It is best to drink bottled or filtered water. Most hotels and riads provide drinking water. Avoid ice from street juice stalls if you have a sensitive stomach.
faq.q9: How much should I tip in Morocco?
faq.a9: Tipping (baksheesh) is appreciated but not always mandatory. Round up taxi fares, leave 5–10% in mid-range restaurants, and tip guides, drivers, and riad staff based on service quality.
faq.q10: What languages are spoken in Morocco?
faq.a10: Arabic (Darija) and Amazigh (Berber) are the official languages. French is widely spoken in cities, administration, and tourism. English is increasingly common in tourist areas, especially among youth and in riads.
faq.q11: How do taxis work in Morocco?
faq.a11: Petit Taxis (city-wide) use meters—insist on using them. Grand Taxis (inter-city) have fixed seat rates. At airports and stations, agree on the fare beforehand or use official ranks. Ride-hailing apps like Careem work in major cities.
faq.q12: Is it safe for women to travel solo in Morocco?
faq.a12: Many women travel solo in Morocco without major issues. Wear modest clothing, ignore persistent calls in medinas, use reliable transport, and prefer riads over isolated areas at night.
faq.q13: Can non-Muslims enter mosques in Morocco?
faq.a13: Most active mosques are closed to non-Muslims. Exceptions include the Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca (guided tours) and some historical sites. Always dress modestly and remove shoes when required.
faq.q14: What type of electrical plugs are used in Morocco?
faq.a14: Morocco uses Type C and E plugs (same as most of Europe) operating at 220V. Travelers from the UK or US should bring a suitable adapter.

tips.label: Good to Know
tips.title: Quick Cultural Tips
tips.tip1_desc: A simple "Salam" or "Bonjour" goes a long way. Use your right hand for eating and passing money. Always ask before photographing people.
tips.tip2_desc: During Ramadan, many restaurants close during the day. Friday is a holy day—some shops open later. Be extra respectful near mosques.
tips.tip3_desc: Always haggle with a smile in the souks. Start around 40-50% of the asking price. Walking away gently often seals a better deal.
